searchText: <vbuterin> So I have some good news: geth people told me that they made some upgrades over the last ~1.5 years and it's *much* faster to make many storage reads now <vbuterin> Basically, I don't think there actually are any known DoS blocks that will take more than a couple seconds to process; if there are, it would be some new crazy quadratic EVM bug <n0ble> These are definitely good news <dankrad> So this acceleration is not based on caches? <vbuterin> It is based on a state cache <dankrad> Because caches are probably easy to game <vbuterin> Different kind of cache <vbuterin> Not "store a few recently used tree nodes", rather "store the entire bottom layer of the state, on disk if needed" <vbuterin> So you need 1 leveldb access to read the state, instead of O(log(n)) <n0ble> you mean to pre-cache something on purpose to further exploit it? (re @dankrad: Because caches are probably easy to game) <n0ble> oh, that’s great! then it’s not actually the cache but a kind of database re-org or optimisation (re @vbuterin: Not "store a few recently used tree nodes", rather "store the entire bottom layer of the state, on disk if needed") <dankrad> hashmaps instead of trees then, I suppose? (re @vbuterin: So you need 1 leveldb access to read the state, instead of O(log(n))) <vbuterin> it's... literally a key/value store <vbuterin> at least that's how I understand it <n0ble> it should enlarge the storage though <vbuterin> right, it does, by ~30 GB <vbuterin> But the tradeoff seems worth it <asqyzeron> The mid-term goal is to keep using these extra 30GB more and more until we no longer need to store the full tree. What about the other clients? <asqyzeron> @paperun my node has synced up to December 30th last year, so I now have an updated list of contracts using DIFFICULTY and BLOCKHASH https://gist.github.com/gballet/fc53f46d4f8e4db2f37a0b64e9b47962 That is the last update, I need the machine for something else. <n0ble> what is the size of the tree? (re @asqyzeron: The mid-term goal is to keep using these extra 30GB more and more until we no longer need to store the full tree.) <vbuterin> 100 GB including that 30, at the moment <vbuterin> (that's total disk storage for the state in the latest version) <n0ble> is this for one or multiple versions of the state? <vbuterin> This is for the current state and a bit of recent history <n0ble> got it, thanks! a quick thought, caches probably useful in the state root computation at the end of the block, which should not result in spikes of block execution time unless there is inadequate number of slots modified during the execution curious, is the current thinking to keep all historic transaction (pre-merge) apart from the merge such that only the state is brought over? if so, how would a user (say in 4 years from now) want to re-verify all of ETH from the ETH1 genesis until that date? are we planning to have the ETH2 client teams make it an option to migrate the history along w/ the state or no? ( I can make the argument for each of those.. ) > how would a user (say in 4 years from now) want to re-verify all of ETH from the ETH1 genesis until that date? I don't think having this functionality is a primary (or necessary) goal. The application layer can choose to not prune pre-merge blocks and have logic to rebuild from genesis, but there are certainly technical debt and other trade-offs here Yeah, it would become a more specialized task: you could run an old ethereum client to verify the ethpow chain up until the end, then you would run an ethereum client to verify the beacon chain under the merge date + 1 month scenario... and a new user now on PoS gets an ETH client, would the idea be that his / her verification from genesis would then be the PoS genesis with one basically massive state block and then all subsequent transactions thereafter? it is an interesting question to ponder.. as I can also imagine a PoS ETH client having the ability to verify from PoW Genesis (which I suppose would then query a PoW client for all its historic blocks).. but then how would the PoS genesis verification occur? i suppose in such a scneario, both PoW and PoS chains from genesis would be able to be verified.... while not really the focus of the merge per se, I do believe many will want to ensure the powchain is somehow retained forever.. purely relying on then legacy clients (which also for sure will have their maintenance decay) may not be the best plan... $0.02 > under the merge date + 1 month scenario... and a new user now on PoS gets an ETH client, would the idea be that his / her verification from genesis would then be the PoS genesis with one basically massive state block and then all subsequent transactions thereafter? yes I think users will have the ability to verify the pow chain if they want to They could just run an eth1 client on it And then they would make two consistency checks: (i) the eth2 genesis actually is what the beacon chain deposit contract generated, and (ii) the state root that gets put into the beacon chain actually is the last state root of the eth1 chain probably more directed at client teams, but i *really* hope we dont have to p2p share a 100gb state.. rather the hash of it to confirm it is correct locally. You can think of the PoS genesis block like a ZK setup ceremony that involved 100s of thousands or millions of people over the course of 6 years. Anyone who joins *after* PoS needs to trust that there was *at least* **one** honest actor in the set of people who were around for the PoS genesis construction/transition. Given the popularity of Ethereum at the moment, I don't think this is at all unreasonable of a trust assumption. <vbuterin> If you validate the PoW chain too, you don't even need that level of trust <vbuterin> (unless of course someone creates an even higher-hashrate PoW chain long after we stop building ours) well I suppose there are really four general options (post-merge).. 1.) use current eth pow clients to have the history 2.) use then eth PoS clients to reference #1 3.) use then PoS client to digest and include #1 in their own db or 4.) hope someone else has the powchain history... I personally fall in the #2 and #3 are the ideal methods with pruning options.. <vbuterin> I guess my preferred camp is "the default behavior should be to run a beacon chain node and a beacon chain node only (the eth1 client would be renamed the "application state library" or something like that), and validating the historic PoW chain would be an optional extra for whoever wants it" <paperun> excellent, ty (re @asqyzeron: @paperun my node has synced up to December 30th last year, so I now have an updated list of contracts using DIFFICULTY and BLOCKHASH https://gist.github.com/gballet/fc53f46d4f8e4db2f37a0b64e9b47962 That is the last update, I need the machine for something else.)

excerpts.author: chat-bridge
excerpts.content: <vbuterin> So I have some good news: geth people told me that they made some upgrades over the last ~1.5 years and it's *much* faster to make many storage reads now

excerpts.author: chat-bridge
excerpts.content: <vbuterin> Basically, I don't think there actually are any known DoS blocks that will take more than a couple seconds to process; if there are, it would be some new crazy quadratic EVM bug

excerpts.author: chat-bridge
excerpts.content: <n0ble> These are definitely good news

excerpts.author: chat-bridge
excerpts.content: <dankrad> So this acceleration is not based on caches?

excerpts.author: chat-bridge
excerpts.content: <vbuterin> It is based on a state cache

excerpts.author: chat-bridge
excerpts.content: <dankrad> Because caches are probably easy to game

excerpts.author: chat-bridge
excerpts.content: <vbuterin> Different kind of cache

excerpts.author: chat-bridge
excerpts.content: <vbuterin> Not "store a few recently used tree nodes", rather "store the entire bottom layer of the state, on disk if needed"

excerpts.author: chat-bridge
excerpts.content: <vbuterin> So you need 1 leveldb access to read the state, instead of O(log(n))

excerpts.author: chat-bridge
excerpts.content: <n0ble> you mean to pre-cache something on purpose to further exploit it? (re @dankrad: Because caches are probably easy to game)

excerpts.author: chat-bridge
excerpts.content: <n0ble> oh, that’s great! then it’s not actually the cache but a kind of database re-org or optimisation (re @vbuterin: Not "store a few recently used tree nodes", rather "store the entire bottom layer of the state, on disk if needed")

excerpts.author: chat-bridge
excerpts.content: <dankrad> hashmaps instead of trees then, I suppose? (re @vbuterin: So you need 1 leveldb access to read the state, instead of O(log(n)))

excerpts.author: chat-bridge
excerpts.content: <vbuterin> it's... literally a key/value store

excerpts.author: chat-bridge
excerpts.content: <vbuterin> at least that's how I understand it

excerpts.author: chat-bridge
excerpts.content: <n0ble> it should enlarge the storage though

excerpts.author: chat-bridge
excerpts.content: <vbuterin> right, it does, by ~30 GB

excerpts.author: chat-bridge
excerpts.content: <vbuterin> But the tradeoff seems worth it

excerpts.author: chat-bridge
excerpts.content: <asqyzeron> The mid-term goal is to keep using these extra 30GB more and more until we no longer need to store the full tree.

excerpts.author: sky.cactus
excerpts.content: What about the other clients?

excerpts.author: chat-bridge

excerpts.author: chat-bridge
excerpts.content: <n0ble> what is the size of the tree? (re @asqyzeron: The mid-term goal is to keep using these extra 30GB more and more until we no longer need to store the full tree.)

excerpts.author: chat-bridge
excerpts.content: <vbuterin> 100 GB including that 30, at the moment

excerpts.author: chat-bridge
excerpts.content: <vbuterin> (that's total disk storage for the state in the latest version)

excerpts.author: chat-bridge
excerpts.content: <n0ble> is this for one or multiple versions of the state?

excerpts.author: chat-bridge
excerpts.content: <vbuterin> This is for the current state and a bit of recent history

excerpts.author: chat-bridge
excerpts.content: <n0ble> got it, thanks! a quick thought, caches probably useful in the state root computation at the end of the block, which should not result in spikes of block execution time unless there is inadequate number of slots modified during the execution

excerpts.author: mrabino1
excerpts.content: curious, is the current thinking to keep all historic transaction (pre-merge) apart from the merge such that only the state is brought over? if so, how would a user (say in 4 years from now) want to re-verify all of ETH from the ETH1 genesis until that date? are we planning to have the ETH2 client teams make it an option to migrate the history along w/ the state or no? ( I can make the argument for each of those.. )

excerpts.author: sky.cactus
excerpts.content:
> how would a user (say in 4 years from now) want to re-verify all of ETH from the ETH1 genesis until that date?
I don't think having this functionality is a primary (or necessary) goal.

excerpts.author: djrtwo
excerpts.content: The application layer can choose to not prune pre-merge blocks and have logic to rebuild from genesis, but there are certainly technical debt and other trade-offs here

excerpts.author: .vbuterin
excerpts.content: Yeah, it would become a more specialized task: you could run an old ethereum client to verify the ethpow chain up until the end, then you would run an ethereum client to verify the beacon chain

excerpts.author: mrabino1
excerpts.content: under the merge date + 1 month scenario... and a new user now on PoS gets an ETH client, would the idea be that his / her verification from genesis would then be the PoS genesis with one basically massive state block and then all subsequent transactions thereafter?  it is an interesting question to ponder.. as I can also imagine a PoS ETH client having the ability to verify from PoW Genesis (which I suppose would then query a PoW client for all its historic blocks).. but then how would the PoS genesis verification occur? i suppose in such a scneario, both PoW and PoS chains from genesis would be able to be verified....   while not really the focus of the merge per se, I do believe many will want to ensure the powchain is somehow retained forever.. purely relying on then legacy clients (which also for sure will have their maintenance decay) may not be the best plan...  $0.02

excerpts.author: .vbuterin
excerpts.content: > under the merge date + 1 month scenario... and a new user now on PoS gets an ETH client, would the idea be that his / her verification from genesis would then be the PoS genesis with one basically massive state block and then all subsequent transactions thereafter?

excerpts.author: .vbuterin
excerpts.content: yes

excerpts.author: .vbuterin
excerpts.content: I think users will have the ability to verify the pow chain if they want to

excerpts.author: .vbuterin
excerpts.content: They could just run an eth1 client on it

excerpts.author: .vbuterin
excerpts.content: And then they would make two consistency checks: (i) the eth2 genesis actually is what the beacon chain deposit contract generated, and (ii) the state root that gets put into the beacon chain actually is the last state root of the eth1 chain

excerpts.author: mrabino1
excerpts.content: probably more directed at client teams, but i *really* hope we dont have to p2p share a 100gb state.. rather the hash of it to confirm it is correct locally.

excerpts.author: sky.cactus
excerpts.content: You can think of the PoS genesis block like a ZK setup ceremony that involved 100s of thousands or millions of people over the course of 6 years.  Anyone who joins *after* PoS needs to trust that there was *at least* **one** honest actor in the set of people who were around for the PoS genesis construction/transition.  Given the popularity of Ethereum at the moment, I don't think this is at all unreasonable of a trust assumption.

excerpts.author: chat-bridge
excerpts.content: <vbuterin> If you validate the PoW chain too, you don't even need that level of trust

excerpts.author: chat-bridge

excerpts.content: well I suppose there are really four general options (post-merge).. 1.) use current eth pow clients to have the history 2.) use then eth PoS clients to reference #1      3.) use then PoS client to digest and include #1 in their own db    or 4.) hope someone else has the powchain history...  I personally fall in the #2 and #3 are the ideal methods with pruning options..

excerpts.author: chat-bridge
excerpts.content: <vbuterin> I guess my preferred camp is "the default behavior should be to run a beacon chain node and a beacon chain node only (the eth1 client would be renamed the "application state library" or something like that), and validating the historic PoW chain would be an optional extra for whoever wants it"
